title: A Saudi-Based Indian Student Just Took CBSE to the Supreme Court. Thousands More Are Stuck.
excerpt: After the Iran war cancelled board exams across seven Gulf nations, one Class 12 student’s results are still missing — and his university deadline has passed.
body:
An Indian student in Saudi Arabia has filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging the Central Board of Secondary Education’s failure to declare his Class 12 results — months after the Iran war forced the cancellation of board exams across seven Gulf nations.

Pransu Jigarkumar Patel, a private candidate who sat for CBSE’s Class 12 improvement examination from Al Jubail in Saudi Arabia, wrote his Physics and Chemistry papers before the board cancelled exams in Mathematics, English, and Computer Science across Bahrain, Iran, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. The cancellations, ordered in March, followed escalating military hostilities in the region that made it unsafe to conduct examinations.

When CBSE declared results on May 13, Patel’s status still read “R.L. (Result Later).” Three representations to the board — on May 17, May 21, and May 30 — went unanswered. His admission application to the B.Tech Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence programme at Dhirubhai Ambani University, filed on May 2, now hangs in limbo.

## A System That Promised a Fix and Didn’t Deliver

CBSE was not caught off guard by the disruption. On March 27, the board issued an “Assessment Scheme for Declaration of Results of Class XII in West Asian Countries” — a framework designed to evaluate students whose exams were cancelled. Under the scheme, students were to be assessed based on their best performance across quarterly, half-yearly, and pre-board examinations, with provisions for special examinations where needed.

For students who completed their exams through the regular cycle, the system worked. Results were declared on time. But for improvement candidates like Patel — students retaking specific subjects to raise their scores — the scheme appears to have broken down. The petition argues that CBSE’s failure to apply its own assessment framework to improvement candidates is “arbitrary, unreasonable, discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.”

## The Scale of the Disruption

Patel’s case has drawn attention because he took it to the highest court in the country, but he is far from alone. Tens of thousands of Indian students attend schools affiliated with CBSE and CISCE boards across the Gulf. The region hosts one of the largest concentrations of Indian expatriate families in the world, with millions of NRIs working in everything from oil and construction to finance and healthcare.

When the Iran war escalated in late February, the disruption rippled through the education system almost immediately. CBSE postponed, then cancelled, board exams for Class 10 and 12 students across all seven affected countries. CISCE followed with its own cancellations. The boards pivoted to internal assessments and alternative evaluations — but parents and education experts have raised persistent concerns about whether these proxy scores will hold weight in competitive college admissions.

For Indian families in the Gulf, the parallels to the 2022 Russia-Ukraine crisis are unsettling. That conflict stranded over 20,000 Indian medical students, most of whom were evacuated under Operation Ganga but returned mid-semester with their academic timelines shattered. Four years later, many are still battling re-admissions, FMGE delays, and lost years. The Iran war now threatens to repeat that pattern at a much larger scale.

## What Happens Next

The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled a hearing in Patel’s case, according to the petition filed through Advocate Raj Kishor Choudhary. But the case puts direct pressure on CBSE to either declare results under its existing assessment scheme or conduct special examinations — and to do so before university admission windows close.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk, who has supported the broader movement for education reform, has said he would undertake a six-week fast if students facing exam-related injustice are not heard.

For the diaspora families who sent their children to the Gulf for quality international schooling, the situation has exposed a gap that no assessment scheme can fully bridge: when the world outside the classroom becomes unsafe, the institutions inside it are not equipped to cope. The Iran war may have started as a geopolitical conflict between nation-states, but its consequences are being felt most acutely in examination halls that will never reopen and on results pages that still say “later.”
